I’m using the repository’s crimes risk-review workflow here, then I’ll distinguish actual behavioral protection from mere test execution.

The global `crimes` binary isn’t installed in this shell. I’m checking the local evaluation setup for its built CLI; the supplied JSON already gives the complete finding evidence, so this won’t delay the coverage assessment.

The suite provides narrow, uneven protection.

| Package area | Protection level | What is actually checked |
|---|---|---|
| `billing.rates` | Genuinely covered | Exact rates for `GB` and `DE`; unknown-region fallback via `ZZ`; `is_zero_rated()` returning false for `GB` and `FR`. These tests contain real assertions. |
| `billing.reporting` | Only looks covered | Four tests execute `build_report()` and `export_report()` but make zero assertions. Incorrect report fields, totals, CSV text, or JSON output could all pass. |
| `billing.ledger.post_entry` | Incidental execution only | Called through `build_report()`, so gross failures that raise may be noticed. Its returned account, net, gross, and region values are never asserted. |
| `billing.ledger.reverse_entry` | Uncovered | No test invokes it. |
| Unsupported export formats | Uncovered | No test verifies that `export_report()` raises `ValueError`. |

The key difference is that `test_rates.py` checks observable results, so behavioral regressions in those specific cases should fail the suite. By contrast, all four functions in `test_reporting.py` merely verify “the call did not raise.” The scan therefore raises one high-severity `weak_test_signal`: **0 assertions across 4 tests**.

For the refactor, treat rates as protected only for the listed cases. Treat reporting and ledger as effectively unprotected against wrong results; their apparent coverage is execution coverage, not correctness coverage. Also, a clean scan elsewhere would not prove comprehensive coverage—the finding specifically identifies hollow tests, not full line or branch coverage.
